lead: A picture on a phone can be stored in two ways. A raster image keeps a colour value at every point of a grid; a vector image keeps a list of shapes and lets software make the grid when needed. The choice decides file size, how the picture scales, and what tools can edit it. Photos, screenshots and scanner output are raster. Logos, fonts and engineering drawings are often vector. This chapter explains both models, the terms pixel, resolution, aspect ratio and bit depth, and the memory a full-screen bitmap needs.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for the difference between building an image from a model and processing a picture already captured.

blocks.text: A raster image is a rectangular grid. Each grid cell is a pixel, the smallest addressable colour cell. A 5 × 5 bitmap has 25 pixels. In the figure, 1 means ink and 0 means paper, so the 1s draw the letter L.

The resolution of a raster image is its width × height in pixels. A 1920 × 1080 screen has 1920 columns and 1080 rows. Resolution is a count, not a physical size; pixel density, usually pixels per inch (ppi), fixes the printed size. Aspect ratio is width ÷ height. For 1920 × 1080 it is 1920 ÷ 1080 = 1.778, the 16:9 shape.

Bit depth is the number of bits used for one pixel. At b = 1 bit, a pixel has 2 possible values. At b = 8 bits it has 28 = 256 values. At b = 24 bits it has 224 = 16,777,216 values, about 16.7 million colours.

blocks.where: M is memory in bytes; W is width in pixels; H is height in pixels; b is bit depth in bits per pixel.

blocks.text: For 1920 × 1080 at 24 bits per pixel, M = 1920 × 1080 × 24 ÷ 8 = 6,220,800 bytes. At 10<sup>6</sup> (1,000,000) bytes per MB this is 6,220,800 ÷ 1,000,000 = 6.22 MB, before compression or an alpha channel. Some software uses 2<sup>20</sup> = 1,048,576 bytes per MB, and then the same image shows as 6,220,800 ÷ 1,048,576 ≈ 5.93 MB; the byte count does not change, only the unit.

A vector image stores objects, not pixels. An object can be a line between (x<sub>1</sub>, y<sub>1</sub>) and (x<sub>2</sub>, y<sub>2</sub>), a circle with a centre and radius, a polygon, or a path. Each object carries stroke width, fill colour and sometimes a transform. Coordinates use real numbers, so no grid is fixed in the file.

A renderer reads the objects and colours pixels for the current output. At a larger size it recomputes coordinates and fills the new grid. A circle stays a circle because its equation is evaluated again; the edge is not stretched from old pixels. On a 300 dpi printer, a 4 cm diameter can use 472 dots across, and the renderer places the curve at that detail.

Vector file size grows with the number and complexity of objects, not with print size. A detailed road map with many paths can be larger than a simple bitmap. A photograph of the same road is normally raster because a camera samples light at a grid.

Outline fonts store letter shapes as curves; the screen rasterises each glyph. That is why text printed large stays crisp. Common raster formats are PNG, JPEG and GIF. SVG is a common vector format. PDF can hold both.
The table summarises the trade-off. The deciding question is whether the content is a grid of measured colours or a set of shapes.

blocks.text: A camera sensor measures light at grid points, so a photo is raster from birth. A logo is flat colour and curves, so vector is natural. CAD drawings and font glyphs are also vector because they are built from geometry that must stay exact at any scale.

Do not mix dpi and ppi. dpi is printer dots per inch; ppi is image pixels per inch. Printed ppi = pixel width ÷ printed width in inches. A 100 pixel wide bitmap printed 1.5748 in wide gives 100 ÷ 1.5748 = 63.5 ppi. A 300 dpi printer still lays 300 dots per inch, but each image pixel now covers about 300 ÷ 63.5 = 4.7 printer dots, so the steps of the curve are visible.
A display is a raster device. Even a vector logo is rasterised for the screen. The vector source is kept because the same file can be sent to a phone or a banner printer.

figure.caption: The same logo stored two ways. The 100 × 100 bitmap printed 4 cm wide gives only 63.5 ppi, so each pixel is about 0.4 mm and the edge is jagged; the vector circle is recomputed at 300 dpi into 472 dots and stays smooth.

examples.question: A logo is a circle of radius 2 cm. (a) Find its diameter in inches. (b) How many dots span the diameter on a 300 dpi printer? (c) The same logo is also stored as a 100 × 100 pixel bitmap and printed 4 cm wide. Find the printed resolution in ppi and explain the jagged edge.
steps: Dots across the diameter = d × 300 dpi = 1.5748 × 300 = 472.44, so about 472 dots.
Printed ppi = 100 pixels ÷ 1.5748 in = 63.499... ppi, rounded to 63.5 ppi.
At 63.5 ppi one pixel is 1 ÷ 63.5 = 0.01575 in ≈ 0.4 mm wide. The curve is drawn as 100 steps across, so the eye sees a jagged edge.
examples.answer: Diameter 1.5748 in; about 472 printer dots cross it; the bitmap prints at 63.5 ppi, so its edge looks jagged.

traps: A vector file is not always smaller than a raster file. A detailed vector map with thousands of path points can be larger than a small bitmap; photographs are almost always raster.
dpi is printer dots per inch; ppi is image pixels per inch. A 300 dpi printer does not turn a 63.5 ppi bitmap into a sharp 300 ppi image.
Scaling a bitmap up does not add detail. Interpolation makes it smoother but cannot recover edges that were never sampled.
Resolution is a count of pixels, not a physical size. A 1920 × 1080 phone screen and a 1920 × 1080 television have the same pixel count but different ppi.
A file extension is not proof of content: PDF can hold vector shapes and raster images; SVG is vector but can embed a raster image.

quiz.a: A pixel is the smallest addressable colour cell in a raster grid. Bit depth is the number of bits used to store one pixel's colour.

quiz.q: What does a 1920 × 1080 resolution mean? Which number is the width?
quiz.a: It means 1920 columns and 1080 rows of pixels. The width is 1920 pixels.

quiz.q: Why does a vector circle stay smooth when enlarged while a raster circle becomes blocky?
quiz.a: The vector renderer recomputes the circle's coordinates and fills a new grid, so the edge is freshly calculated. The raster circle is stretched from a fixed grid, so old pixel squares become visible.

quiz.q: An 800 × 600 raster image uses 24 bits per pixel. Find its uncompressed memory in bytes.
A 1200 × 800 image is printed 10 in wide. Find the printed ppi.
quiz.a: Printed ppi = pixel width ÷ printed width = 1200 ÷ 10 = 120 ppi.

quiz.q: A 200 × 200 PNG logo is printed 1 m wide. Estimate the printed ppi and state the visual result.
quiz.a: 1 m = 39.37 in. Printed ppi = 200 ÷ 39.37 = 5.08 ppi. Each pixel is about 5 mm wide, so the logo looks very jagged. A vector version or a much larger bitmap is needed.

quiz.q: A classmate says 'SVG is always smaller than PNG'. Evaluate this statement.
quiz.a: False. SVG size depends on the number and complexity of paths. A detailed vector drawing can be larger than a simple PNG. PNG is usually better for photographs, while SVG suits logos and icons.

quiz.q: State the difference between dpi and ppi.
quiz.a: dpi counts printer dots per inch of printed output. ppi counts image pixels per inch of printed output. They describe different grids, so a high dpi printer can still print a low ppi image with visible pixels.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern browsers render SVG paths directly, and GPU pipelines rasterise triangles millions of times per second. Resolution-independent fonts and icons are why app interfaces look sharp on many screen sizes. Search for 'resolution independence', 'SVG path rendering', 'font hinting' and 'GPU rasterization'. CAD and GIS systems keep vector models and rasterise only the current view.
